text.long_definition: OAuth lets one app get limited access to your account on another service without ever seeing your password. think of a prescription transfer: the patient authorizes you to pull their rx history from another pharmacy, and that pharmacy hands over just the specific records — never the patient's login to their chart. in an OAuth sign-in, the app sends you to a trusted identity provider like Google, you approve, and the app receives a token (a short proof of permission) instead of your password.

text.long_definition: RBAC stands for role-based access control. Instead of deciding permissions one person at a time, the system defines roles — like how your EHR gives nurses, physicians, pharmacists, and unit clerks each a different set of things they can see and do — and every user gets assigned a role that carries those permissions. text.long_definition: a join combines rows from two separate tables by matching them on a shared piece of information. think of how the EHR links a patient's room number to their full chart: the room assignment list and the patient chart live in different places, but they share a patient ID, so the system can pull them together into one view.

text.long_definition: an HTTP header is extra information attached to a web request or response, separate from the main content. headers can say things like what format the sender expects back, what login token proves who's asking, whether the answer is allowed to be reused later, or where the request came from. think of it like the label stapled to a prescription bag: the pills are the main thing, but the label carries the patient name, the prescriber, the fill date, and the warnings the next person needs to handle it correctly.
text.why_it_matters: a lot of invisible web behavior lives in headers: which login token is being sent, what content type is accepted, whether a response can be reused from cache, which site the request came from. when something works on one computer and fails on another, a missing or wrong header is often the reason — which is why help desk sometimes asks about them.
text.example_in_sentence: the release notes said the pharmacy system now requires a new authorization HTTP header on every request so the server knows which store is calling.

text.long_definition: a payload is the actual useful data being carried inside something larger. an API request, a webhook, a token, or a log entry all have an outer wrapper (addressing info, headers, routing details) plus the real contents the receiver cares about. the payload is those real contents. think of it like the SBAR content inside a handoff: the shift, room number, and sender are the wrapper; the patient info is what the next nurse actually needs.

text.long_definition: When you see a model described as "70B" or "405B," the "B" means billion parameters. Parameters are the internal settings the model adjusted during training — billions of tiny numerical dials that together encode what it knows. More parameters generally mean better answers but slower responses and higher cost each time you use it. The biggest open models (Llama 405B) and frontier models (Claude, GPT-5) sit in the hundreds of billions of parameters.
text.why_it_matters: Product names like "GPT-5," "Claude Opus 4.7," "Gemini 2.5 Pro," or "Llama 405B" start to make sense once you know the "B" is billions of parameters. It is the simplest rough gauge of a model's heft, though parameter count alone does not fully predict quality.
text.example_in_sentence: Llama 3 70B has 70 billion parameters — smaller than Claude but light enough to run on a laptop.

text.long_definition: a calculated column adds a new column to a table in the data model, where the value for each row is figured out once using a formula (written in a Power BI formula language called DAX) and then stored. it's different from a measure, which is a formula that gets recalculated on the fly depending on what the user is filtering or looking at in the report.
text.why_it_matters: a calculated column is computed once per row and frozen in, while a measure recalculates every time someone filters or slices the report. picking the wrong one is a common Power BI mistake — if you use a column where you needed a measure, your totals won't update when the user changes the view, and the numbers in a dashboard can quietly go wrong.
text.example_in_sentence: the analyst built a calculated column to tag each patient visit as inpatient or observation, since that label never changes once the row lands in the table.

text.long_definition: encryption scrambles readable data into gibberish using a key, so only someone with the matching key can turn it back into something readable. it protects data moving across a network (like a website session) and data sitting in storage (like a backup file). without the key, the scrambled version is useless.
text.why_it_matters: this is what makes a stolen laptop or a lost backup drive a non-event instead of a patient-data breach. when the help desk says traffic is "protected in transit" or a backup is "safe to store," encryption is the mechanism doing the work. the flip side: if the key is lost, the data is gone for good too.

text.long_definition: CDN stands for content delivery network. Instead of every user downloading images, scripts, and other static files from one central server, a CDN keeps copies of those files on servers scattered around the country and world.
